positions.claim: Controlling burn at the point of individual purchase approval is the wrong mechanism; spending review must happen earlier, at the budgeting stage.
Speed determines startup success or failure, and speed is determined by operational infrastructure rather than by team intelligence.
Deep tech companies usually fail because they cannot organize human organizations, not because the technology doesn't work.
The four-stage funnel (company-wide vote, phone screen, homework, full interview) is the minimum set of steps needed to make a hiring decision — there is no more efficient process.
Interview-to-offer conversion should be at least 25%, or on-sites waste too much of the team's time.
Take-homes should be made AI-resistant through non-saturating, high-ceiling, numerically scorable tasks; candidates' use of AI models is otherwise irrelevant.
Annual 360 performance reviews are disruptive and mostly resurface known problems; continuous peer voting weighted by eigenvector centrality is more or less the right way to do performance reviews.
When two approaches are otherwise comparable, choose the one with the shorter iteration cycle because compounding dominates other advantages.
A CEO cannot delegate judgment and must make decisions that make sense to them regardless of the momentum behind alternatives.
For most fields, working at a high-performing company adjacent to your target area is better preparation than getting a PhD, because startup culture is an oral tradition you learn by doing.
The best evidence of exceptional ability is winning legible competitive games; it is hard to know you're exceptional without one.

A small team that can hold more of an interdisciplinary problem in their heads outperforms academia's model of deep verticalized experts meeting at an interdisciplinary center, because the latter ships the interfaces between departments.
AI agents have so far been a multiplier for the team rather than a replacement, with the biggest impact in coding and regulatory/quality-system work.
AI and regulation are a better fit than people think — most regulations are written in blood and largely good ideas, and the real bottleneck is humans being bad at reading and interpreting standards.
Companies should build internal software rather than buy it; commercial ERP and ATS products force bottlenecks and nobody loves them, and agents have made building viable.
Founders should price out the experiments needed to reach the next value inflection point and raise twice that amount; keeping waste to 20-30% is a good outcome.
Founders should push for profitability sooner than they think they need to, even in long-horizon deep tech.
In the near term BCI is a longevity and healthcare story rather than an AI story, because neural engineering delivers effect sizes medicine otherwise can't reach.
Consciousness is a practical problem, not a philosophical one — a BCI that could read and drive every neuron would let us figure it out quickly.
Biotech remains capital intensive and he would not recommend it to someone with other options, though the patient impact when it works is unlike any other sector.
A company needs both mission zealots and pragmatic professionals — roughly 20/80 at SpaceX, 30/70 at Science — to succeed over the long term.
Roughly half of a deep tech startup's burn is headcount, leaving about $3M/year of research budget on a $20M Series A.
